original.text: aśaktir aparijñānaṃ kramakopo 'tha vā punaḥ / evaṃ hi sarvathā buddhair ajātiḥ paridīpitā
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'māṇḍūkyopaniṣatkārikā' (via the DCS corpus), sources_raw/prepared/mandukya-karika
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — verse-level quotation with attribution

paraphrase: Inability (of a cause to produce), non-apprehension (of origination) and the violation of sequence (of cause and effect): in these ways non-origination has been made manifest in every way by the awakened (buddhaiḥ).
notes: Kārikā numbering as in the GRETIL/DCS e-text (prakaraṇa.verse), which matches the common editions for book 4. 'buddhaiḥ' is read by Śaṅkara as 'by the wise'; many modern readers take it as a reference to Buddhist teachers. Both readings recorded; no verdict.

original.text: upalambhāt samācārād asti vastutvavādinām / jātis tu deśitā buddhair ajātes trasatāṃ sadā
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'māṇḍūkyopaniṣatkārikā' (via the DCS corpus), sources_raw/prepared/mandukya-karika
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — verse-level quotation with attribution

paraphrase: Origination was taught by the awakened (buddhaiḥ) — on account of perception and of conventional practice — for those who hold that things are real and who always fear non-origination.
notes: Kārikā numbering as in the GRETIL/DCS e-text (prakaraṇa.verse), which matches the common editions for book 4. A teaching of provisional instruction for those who fear the ultimate — cf. the Buddhist doctrine of skilful means; the parallel is recorded in brw:mahayana-vocabulary-in-alatasanti.

original.text: yo 'sti kalpitasaṃvṛtyā paramārthena nāsty asau / paratantrābhisaṃvṛtyā syān nāsti paramārthataḥ // ajaḥ kalpitasaṃvṛtyā paramārthena nāpy ajaḥ / paratantrādiniṣpattyā saṃvṛtyā jāyate tu saḥ
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'māṇḍūkyopaniṣatkārikā' (via the DCS corpus), sources_raw/prepared/mandukya-karika
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — verse-level quotation with attribution

paraphrase: What exists by imagined convention (kalpita-saṃvṛti) does not exist in the ultimate sense; what may exist by the convention of dependence on others (paratantra) does not exist ultimately. The unborn is unborn by imagined convention, not even unborn in the ultimate sense; by convention it is (said to be) born through dependence on others and the rest.
notes: Kārikā numbering as in the GRETIL/DCS e-text (prakaraṇa.verse), which matches the common editions for book 4. The terms kalpita, paratantra and saṃvṛti are also the terms of the Yogācāra three natures and of the Buddhist two truths (recorded as shared vocabulary, brw:mahayana-vocabulary-in-alatasanti).

original.text: savastu sopalambhaṃ ca dvayaṃ laukikam iṣyate / avastu sopalambhaṃ ca śuddhaṃ laukikam iṣyate // avastv anupalambhaṃ ca lokottaram iti smṛtam / jñānaṃ jñeyaṃ ca vijñeyaṃ sadā buddhaiḥ prakīrtitam
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'māṇḍūkyopaniṣatkārikā' (via the DCS corpus), sources_raw/prepared/mandukya-karika
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — verse-level quotation with attribution

paraphrase: Duality with an object and with apprehension is held to be the worldly (laukika); apprehension without an object is the pure worldly (śuddha-laukika); without object and without apprehension is remembered as the supramundane (lokottara). Knowledge and the knowable (in these three) have always been proclaimed by the awakened.
notes: Kārikā numbering as in the GRETIL/DCS e-text (prakaraṇa.verse), which matches the common editions for book 4. Three grades of cognition (waking, dream, and the state without object or apprehension); 'lokottara' is a common Buddhist term.

original.text: heyajñeyāpyapākyāni vijñeyāny agrayāṇataḥ / teṣām anyatra vijñeyād upalambhas triṣu smṛtaḥ
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'māṇḍūkyopaniṣatkārikā' (via the DCS corpus), sources_raw/prepared/mandukya-karika
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — verse-level quotation with attribution

paraphrase: What is to be abandoned, known, attained and brought to maturity are to be understood from the foremost vehicle (agrayāna); of these, apart from the knowable (the ultimate), the other three are held to be mere apprehension.
notes: Kārikā numbering as in the GRETIL/DCS e-text (prakaraṇa.verse), which matches the common editions for book 4. 'agrayāna' is otherwise a Mahāyāna self-designation; Śaṅkara glosses it as the foremost means (upāya). The construal of the second line is uncertain (moderate confidence).

original.text: alabdhāvaraṇāḥ sarve dharmāḥ prakṛtinirmalāḥ / ādau buddhās tathā muktā budhyanta iti nāyakāḥ
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'māṇḍūkyopaniṣatkārikā' (via the DCS corpus), sources_raw/prepared/mandukya-karika
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — verse-level quotation with attribution

paraphrase: All dharmas are free of any covering and pure by nature; they are awakened (buddhāḥ) and liberated from the beginning — so the leaders understand.
notes: Kārikā numbering as in the GRETIL/DCS e-text (prakaraṇa.verse), which matches the common editions for book 4. 'dharma', 'prakṛti-nirmala' and 'ādau buddhāḥ' echo Mahāyāna and Buddha-nature language; Advaita reads dharma as the selves (jīvas) identical with Brahman.

original.text: durdarśam atigambhīram ajaṃ sāmyaṃ viśāradam / buddhvā padam anānātvaṃ namaskurmo yathābalam
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'māṇḍūkyopaniṣatkārikā' (via the DCS corpus), sources_raw/prepared/mandukya-karika
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — verse-level quotation with attribution

paraphrase: Having realized that state which is hard to see, very deep, unborn, the same, pure and without multiplicity, we pay homage to it as best we can.
notes: Kārikā numbering as in the GRETIL/DCS e-text (prakaraṇa.verse), which matches the common editions for book 4.

paraphrase: On 'this was not spoken by the Buddha': the non-dual reality, free of the distinctions of knower, knowing and known, was not taught by the Buddha; although the Buddhist denial of external objects and the doctrine of mere cognition come close to non-duality, this non-dual reality is to be known only from the Upaniṣads.
notes: Gist recalled (the commentary ascribed to Śaṅkara); no original given. The Advaita tradition's own denial of Buddhist dependence.

paraphrase: Arāḍa: nature (prakṛti) and modification (vikāra), birth, death and old age — that is called 'the being'. Know as prakṛti the five elements, the I-maker (ahaṃkāra), intellect (buddhi) and the unmanifest; as modifications, the objects, the senses, hands, feet, speech, anus, genitals and mind. Because it knows this field it is called the field-knower (kṣetrajña), and those who reflect on the self call the self the field-knower. Kapila with his disciple is remembered here as the awakened (pratibuddha); Prajāpati with his sons as the unawakened. What is born, ages, is afflicted and dies is the manifest; the unmanifest is its opposite.
speaker: Arāḍa Kālāma
notes: Canto.verse as in Johnston's numbering (SARIT e-text). Arāḍa's teaching is as Aśvaghoṣa, a Buddhist poet, presents it. Variant readings in the e-text (e.g. prakṛtiṃ/prakṛtir, pratibuddhir/pratibuddha) do not change the sense.

paraphrase: Ignorance, action and craving are to be known as the causes of saṃsāra; the being standing in these three does not pass beyond that state.
speaker: Arāḍa Kālāma
notes: Canto.verse as in Johnston's numbering (SARIT e-text). Arāḍa's teaching is as Aśvaghoṣa, a Buddhist poet, presents it.

original.text: tamo mohaṃ mahāmohaṃ tāmisradvayam eva ca
original.edition: Buddhacarita, SARIT markdown e-text (Johnston's text with variants), sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/sarit-markdown/asvaghosa-buddhacarita.md; IAST by the unit

paraphrase: Arāḍa: the ignorant one exerts himself in a five-jointed ignorance — darkness (tamas), delusion (moha), great delusion (mahāmoha) and the two blindnesses (tāmisra, andhatāmisra). Darkness is sloth; delusion is birth and death; great delusion is desire; tāmisra is anger; andhatāmisra is despondency. Joined with this five-jointed ignorance the fool is poured into births in a saṃsāra full of suffering.
speaker: Arāḍa Kālāma
notes: Canto.verse as in Johnston's numbering (SARIT e-text). Arāḍa's teaching is as Aśvaghoṣa, a Buddhist poet, presents it. The same five names are the five 'misconceptions' (viparyaya) of Sāṃkhyakārikā 47–48 and correspond to the five afflictions of YS 2.3; see brw:samkhya-in-buddhacarita.

paraphrase: Arāḍa: the one who seeks liberation should know the four — the awakened and the unawakened, the manifest and the unmanifest; knowing these correctly the field-knower leaves the round of births and attains the imperishable state. For this purpose brahmins who teach the supreme Brahman practise the holy life (brahmacarya) and make others do so.
speaker: Arāḍa Kālāma
notes: Canto.verse as in Johnston's numbering (SARIT e-text). Arāḍa's teaching is as Aśvaghoṣa, a Buddhist poet, presents it.

paraphrase: Arāḍa's path: leaving home, taking the mendicant's sign and moral conduct, contentment and solitude, seeing danger in passion, he restrains the senses; secluded from desires and ill will he attains the first meditation with reasoning (vitarka); then the second with joy and pleasure, the third with pleasure without joy, the fourth free of pleasure and pain. Some, satisfied, take each attainment for liberation and reach the corresponding heavens (Brahmā's world, the radiant gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Bṛhatphala gods).
speaker: Arāḍa Kālāma
notes: Canto.verse as in Johnston's numbering (SARIT e-text). Arāḍa's teaching is as Aśvaghoṣa, a Buddhist poet, presents it. Arāḍa's path is given in the Buddhist vocabulary of the four jhānas and their heavens.

original.text: tato muñjād iṣīkeva śakuniḥ pañjarād iva / kṣetrajño niḥsṛto dehān mukta ity abhidhīyate // etat tat paramaṃ brahma nirliṅgaṃ dhruvam akṣaram / yan mokṣa iti tattvajñāḥ kathayanti manīṣiṇaḥ
original.edition: Buddhacarita, SARIT markdown e-text (Johnston's text with variants), sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/sarit-markdown/asvaghosa-buddhacarita.md; IAST by the unit

paraphrase: Arāḍa: detached even from form, the wise one first imagines the spaces of the body as space, then attains the sphere of space; another, turning the self back by the self and seeing 'there is nothing', is called the one of nothingness (ākiñcanya). Then, like a reed from its sheath or a bird from its cage, the field-knower goes out from the body and is called liberated. This is the supreme Brahman, without mark, constant, imperishable, which the knowers of reality call liberation.
speaker: Arāḍa Kālāma
notes: Canto.verse as in Johnston's numbering (SARIT e-text). Arāḍa's teaching is as Aśvaghoṣa, a Buddhist poet, presents it.

paraphrase: Arāḍa: Jaigīṣavya, Janaka, the elder Parāśara and other seekers of liberation were freed by reaching this path.
speaker: Arāḍa Kālāma
notes: Canto.verse as in Johnston's numbering (SARIT e-text). Arāḍa's teaching is as Aśvaghoṣa, a Buddhist poet, presents it. Jaigīṣavya is a Sāṃkhya-Yoga teacher cited in the Yogabhāṣya; Janaka and Parāśara appear as teachers of liberation in the Mokṣadharma.

original.text: parataḥ paratas tyāgo yasmāt tu guṇavān smṛtaḥ / tasmāt sarvaparityāgān manye kṛtsnāṃ kṛtārthatām
original.edition: Buddhacarita, SARIT markdown e-text (Johnston's text with variants), sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/sarit-markdown/asvaghosa-buddhacarita.md; IAST by the unit

paraphrase: The bodhisattva's reply: this subtle knowledge, auspicious beyond the higher, is not final, because the field-knower is not given up. The field-knower, though freed from nature and modifications, still has the nature of producing and of a seed; as long as a self remains, the relinquishing of ignorance, action and craving is not complete, and the freedom from I-making is only imagined; if the self is a knower it has something to know and is not freed, if not a knower a posited self is useless. Because relinquishing is called complete only when everything is relinquished, I hold that total relinquishment is the full accomplishment.
speaker: the bodhisattva
notes: Canto.verse as in Johnston's numbering (SARIT e-text). Arāḍa's teaching is as Aśvaghoṣa, a Buddhist poet, presents it. Original quoted: 12.82. Some verses (12.71–73) are bracketed in the e-text as doubtful.

paraphrase: Wishing to hear something higher, the bodhisattva went to Udraka's hermitage but did not accept his view either, because of its grasping at a self: Udraka, seeing the fault of both perception and non-perception, had gone beyond nothingness to the state that is neither perception nor non-perception; but since one returns (to the world) even after reaching it, the bodhisattva left him.
notes: Canto.verse as in Johnston's numbering (SARIT e-text). Arāḍa's teaching is as Aśvaghoṣa, a Buddhist poet, presents it.

original.text: Mayampi kho, āvuso, sāvakānaṁ evaṁ dhammaṁ desema
original.licence: Pali root text public domain; SuttaCentral Mahāsaṅgīti edition (bilara-data), CC0

paraphrase: Wanderers of other sects tell the monks at Haliddavasana: 'The ascetic Gotama teaches his disciples to abandon the five hindrances, the defilements of mind that weaken wisdom, and to dwell pervading one direction, then all directions, with a mind of love, of compassion, of rejoicing and of equanimity. We too teach our disciples thus. What then is the difference between his teaching and ours?'
notes: SuttaCentral segment numbers sn46.54:3.1–15.10. A Buddhist text reporting that other ascetic communities taught the abandoning of the hindrances and the four immeasurables.

original.text: Subhaparamāhaṁ, bhikkhave, mettācetovimuttiṁ vadāmi, idhapaññassa bhikkhuno uttarivimuttiṁ appaṭivijjhato
original.licence: Pali root text public domain; SuttaCentral Mahāsaṅgīti edition (bilara-data), CC0

paraphrase: The Buddha's answer: ask them how each liberation of mind is developed, what is its destination, culmination, fruit and end — they cannot answer. The liberation of mind by love culminates in the beautiful (subha); by compassion, in the sphere of infinite space; by rejoicing, in the sphere of infinite consciousness; by equanimity, in the sphere of nothingness — for a monk who has not penetrated a higher liberation.
notes: SuttaCentral segment numbers sn46.54:3.1–15.10.

paraphrase: (Commentary:) the tenets of all philosophies, from the Cārvākas on, are roles assumed at will by the one self, like an actor's: the Cārvākas take the body qualified by consciousness as the self; the Naiyāyikas and others a self that is practically the intellect, and in liberation practically a void; the Mīmāṃsakas also rest in the intellect; the Buddhists (saugata), who hold the stream of cognitions to be reality, end in the activities of the intellect; some Vedāntins take breath as the self, others rest in the void or in the Lord-principle; the Mādhyamikas likewise; the Pāñcarātrikas cling to the unmanifest; the Sāṃkhyas stand on a level like that of the vijñānākalas; the grammarians rest at the level of Sadāśiva; the Tāntrikas hold the self transcendent, the Kula systems immanent, the Trika both. All these are stages of the one conscious Lord, differing by the degree to which his freedom is concealed or revealed.
notes: Kṣemarāja's own commentary on sūtra 8, GRETIL KSTS text (sources_raw/prepared/pratyabhijnahrdaya); the ontology's source id for the work is src:pratyabhijnahrdayam.

original.text: buddhitattve sthitā bauddhā guṇeṣv evārhatāḥ sthitāḥ / sthitā vedavidaḥ puṃsi avyakte pāñcarātrikāḥ
original.edition: Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya with Kṣemarāja's commentary, GRETIL (KSTS text), sources_raw/prepared/pratyabhijnahrdaya
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — verse-level quotation with attribution

paraphrase: (Commentary, citing the āgamas:) 'The Buddhists abide in the intellect-principle, the Ārhatas (Jains) in the qualities, the knowers of the Veda in the Person, the Pāñcarātrikas in the unmanifest.'
notes: Kṣemarāja's own commentary on sūtra 8, GRETIL KSTS text (sources_raw/prepared/pratyabhijnahrdaya); the ontology's source id for the work is src:pratyabhijnahrdayam. Kṣemarāja introduces it with 'etac ca āgameṣu … nirūpitam'; the exact āgama is not named here (to be identified in Phase C).

original.text: dpal he ru ka la phyag 'tshal lo/ /spyan gsum rab ldan dbu bcad sku mdog dmar/
original.edition: Derge Tengyur, Tōh 2285, digital edition by Esukhia and Barom Theksum Choling (sources_raw/derge-tengyur), folio 142b.7–145a.1
original.licence: Public domain (Derge xylograph; Esukhia/Barom digital edition, per the repository)

paraphrase: The Tibetan opens: 'Homage to Śrī Heruka' and praises a red, three-eyed, head-severed deity who dispels the fear of death and holds the seal (mudrā) of yogins and yoginīs; it then announces that the 'great seals' (phyag rgya chen po) will be explained, whose mere hearing makes a person honoured by all the gods, and begins with the seated practice in which the left heel blocks the anus and the right leg is extended.
notes: Derge Tengyur Tōh 2285, 142b.7–145a.1 (Tibetan; paraphrase says what the Tibetan reads). The practice named is the haṭha 'mahāmudrā'; summarized only. The head-severed red deity is the iconography of Chinnamuṇḍā-Vajravārāhī (identification by the unit; the text gives no name).

original.text: bdud rtsi grub pa zhes bya ba slob dpon chen po bi rU pas mdzad pa rdzogs so
original.edition: Derge Tengyur, Tōh 2285, digital edition by Esukhia and Barom Theksum Choling (sources_raw/derge-tengyur), folio 142b.7–145a.1
original.licence: Public domain (Derge xylograph; Esukhia/Barom digital edition, per the repository)

paraphrase: The colophon reads: 'The Amṛtasiddhi composed by the great master Virūpa is complete', and says it was translated by an Indian master, a yogin who had attained siddhi.
notes: Derge Tengyur Tōh 2285, 142b.7–145a.1 (Tibetan; paraphrase says what the Tibetan reads). Evidence for the Buddhist transmission and attribution of the Amṛtasiddhi corpus (brw:amrtasiddhi-buddhist-to-hatha).

paraphrase: (Śrīharṣa, answering the charge that his method is the Mādhyamika's:) the Saugata (Mādhyamika) and the Brahma-vādin agree that the world of difference cannot be determined as existent or non-existent; they differ in that the former declares everything, consciousness included, indeterminable, while the Brahma-vādins hold that the universe other than consciousness is different from both being and non-being.
notes: Recalled; exact locus in the first pariccheda to be fixed in Phase C. An Advaitin's own acknowledgement of methodological affinity with Madhyamaka together with a stated difference.

location.section: Uttarakhaṇḍa (the chapter classifying the Purāṇas and śāstras by guṇa)

paraphrase: Śiva tells Pārvatī that the doctrine of illusion (māyāvāda) is a false scripture, called 'Buddhism in disguise' (pracchanna bauddha), and that he himself propounds it in the Kali age in the form of a brahmin.
speaker: Śiva
notes: The verse is quoted by Vaiṣṇava and other critics of Advaita (e.g. Vijñānabhikṣu, the Gauḍīyas); its verse number differs between editions (low confidence on the ref). A polemical text, recorded for dsp:advaita-crypto-buddhism, not a verdict.

paraphrase: In the second part (Trailokyavijaya), Vajrapāṇi, in the wrathful form 'Conqueror of the Three Worlds', is charged by Vairocana with bringing Maheśvara and the other worldly gods into the maṇḍala; Maheśvara resists, is subdued and dies, and is revived (in another world) as a buddha; the gods are then given places and new names in the maṇḍala.
notes: Recalled at section level; details (the name under which Maheśvara is revived) to be checked.

paraphrase: In the examination of inference Śāntarakṣita sets out and answers the view of the Jain Pātrasvāmin that the single mark of a valid reason is its 'otherwise-impossibility' (anyathānupapannatva): where it is present, what use are the three characteristics? where it is absent, what use are the three?
notes: Verse numbers recalled only approximately (c. TS 1364–1380); gist moderate confidence.
reporting_source: src:tattvasangraha (Buddhist report of a Jain view)

paraphrase: The Maithili Varṇaratnākara includes, among its stock lists, a list of eighty-four siddhas that mixes names known from the Nāth tradition (Mīnanātha, Gorakṣanātha, Cauraṅgīnātha) with names known from the Buddhist siddha lists (among them Virūpa, Kāṇha, Jālandhara, Nāgārjuna, Carpaṭi).
notes: Recalled from secondary descriptions; the exact names, order and count must be checked against the edition (Chatterji & Mishra). Flagged in REPORT.md.
